name: Maya (Classic period)
summary: The Classic Maya built great city-states with a full writing system, advanced calendars and astronomy, before many southern cities were abandoned in the 9th century.

knownFor.label: Long Count calendar
knownFor.note: A calendar counting days from a starting date in 3114 BCE.

knownFor.label: Tikal temples
knownFor.note: Tall stepped pyramids in the rainforest.

knownFor.label: Cacao drink
knownFor.note: Chocolate was drunk by the elite.

location.value: Southeastern Mexico (Yucatán, Chiapas), Guatemala, Belize and western Honduras and El Salvador.

terrain.value: Tropical lowland forests (Petén) and volcanic highlands, with few rivers in the north (people relied on cenotes, natural sinkholes).

climate.value: Tropical, with dry and rainy seasons. Severe droughts are one proposed cause of the 9th-century collapse.

resources.value: Maize, beans, squash, cacao, jade, obsidian and salt.

disasters.value: Droughts and environmental degradation are suggested factors in the collapse. These are debated.

population.value: Not stated in the Wikipedia infobox. The largest Classic cities may have had 50,000–120,000 people.

urbanisation.value: Many city-states, including Tikal, Calakmul, Copán, Palenque and later Chichen Itza.

disease.value: Epidemics brought by Europeans after 1511 devastated Maya populations.

migration.value: After the 9th-century collapse, populations shifted north to Yucatán. Today over 6 million Maya people speak about 28 Mayan languages.

economicBase.value: Farming (maize, beans, squash), plus crafts and trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade networks across Mesoamerica in obsidian, jade, salt, cacao and feathers. Chichen Itza imported gold from Central America.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; jade, cacao and quetzal feathers were luxury goods.

moneyAndTax.value: Cacao beans and cloth were used as money (not exclusively). Tribute was paid to rulers.

inequality.value: Divine kings and nobles above commoners, who were over 90% of the population.

governmentType.value: Independent city-states ruled by “divine kings” (kʼuhul ajaw). Joint council rule appeared in the Postclassic.

keyRulers.value: Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal of Palenque (615–683). Yuknoom Chʼeen II of Calakmul. Jasaw Chan Kʼawiil I of Tikal.

succession.value: Usually from father to son; a few women ruled, such as Lady Six Sky of Naranjo.

institutions.value: Royal courts, scribes, temple priesthoods, and alliances between cities.

stability.value: Frequent wars between city-states. Tikal and Calakmul were great rivals.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry and war among dynasties. Civil wars accompanied the 9th-century collapse.

armyAndTech.value: Warriors with spears, atlatls (spear-throwers) and obsidian weapons. Raids took captives for sacrifice.

majorWars.value: The Tikal–Calakmul wars (6th–7th centuries). The Spanish conquest (1520s–1697).

territoryChange.value: No single empire. Power shifted between city-states. The last independent Maya city, Nojpetén, fell in 1697.

alliancesRivals.value: City alliances. Teotihuacan intervened in Maya politics (e.g. at Tikal, 378).

inventions.value: The most developed writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas, the Long Count calendar, one of the earliest known zeros, and raised causeways (sacbeob).

scienceEducation.value: Scribes made careful astronomical observations in the codices; the Dresden Codex devotes six pages to calculating the rising and positions of Venus.

openness.value: Interacted with Teotihuacan and other Mesoamerican peoples.

communicationTransport.value: Raised white stone roads (sacbeob) linked cities; canoes along the coast and rivers; no wheeled transport or pack animals.

religion.value: Polytheistic, with rituals of bloodletting and sacrifice, the ballgame, and the 260-day sacred calendar (still used in Highland Guatemala).

languageWriting.value: Mayan languages, written in a hieroglyphic script (largely deciphered since the 1950s–80s).

artsArchitecture.value: Stepped pyramids and palaces (Tikal, Palenque, Chichen Itza), carved stelae, murals (Bonampak) and painted pottery.

socialStructure.value: Kings, nobles, priests, scribes, merchants, farmers and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared culture and calendar across many independent cities. Maya identity remains strong today.

dailyLife.value: Thatched houses of wood and mud on stone platforms; maize tortillas, beans, squash, chili and cacao drinks for the elite.

neighbours.value: Teotihuacan, Zapotecs, Olmecs (earlier), Toltecs and the Aztecs.

colonisation.value: Colonised by Spain from the 1520s, a process that took until 1697.

riseSignals.value: Farming villages, then cities by about 750 BCE, writing by the 3rd century BCE, and trade and dynastic monuments from about 250 CE.

declineSignals.value: Warfare, overpopulation and environmental damage, and drought. No single theory is accepted.

outcome.value: Collapse in the southern lowlands in the 9th century. Postclassic cities continued in the north and highlands until the Spanish conquest (completed 1697).

sources.value: Hieroglyphic inscriptions, a few surviving codices, archaeology, and colonial Spanish and Maya accounts (the Popol Vuh). Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Coe & Houston (2015).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Writing is largely deciphered. The causes of the collapse and population figures are debated. This entry covers the Classic period (250–900); Maya civilisation spans c. 2000 BCE – 1697 CE. Second source: Wikidata covers all of Maya civilisation (2000 BCE–1521); this app covers the Classic period (250–900).
